# Small Models, Big Bets: What We’ve Learned Building SLMs at India’s Largest Private Bank


[HDFC Bank Tech Blog](https://medium.com/@tech.insights_44381?source=post_page---byline--b403c7f8a927-----------------------------------------)

*Bigger isn’t always better. In the applications we’ve evaluated, specialised small language models are showing cost reductions of approximately 20–40% — and changing how we build enterprise AI.*


For a while now, the AI story has been told in one direction: up. More parameters. More GPUs. More money. Every new frontier model arrives with a bigger number attached, and the message to enterprises has been simple — rent the biggest brain you can afford.


That isn’t quite how it has played out for us. We build AI at HDFC Bank, India’s largest private bank. When you run AI in production across real enterprise workflows, “biggest” stops being the obvious answer.


So this is our attempt to write down what we’ve learned so far about small language models (SLMs): where *small* wins, where it doesn’t, and why we think the real skill is knowing the difference. It’s not a rejection of frontier AI. It’s a practical, numbers-first view from the team doing the work.


## It’s not David vs. Goliath. It’s a team sport.


Are we moving to SLMs instead of LLMs? The short answer is no. We’re investing in SLMs, but *not instead of* frontier models.


The way we think about it is what the industry has started calling **compound AI** — systems that stitch together multiple models, tools, data sources and workflows to answer a single user request.

Consider what actually happens when a customer asks one of our assistants something mildly complicated. The system has to:


1. Figure out what the customer wants
2. Decide which tool or system to call
3. Retrieve the right data
4. Apply business rules and compliance checks
5. Run a calculation
6. Write a clear, accurate reply


A frontier-scale model is not necessary — or optimal — for every one of those steps. Routing an intent into a fixed set of categories is not the same problem as reasoning through an ambiguous complaint.


So we pick the model per step, weighing **complexity, required accuracy, latency, cost and privacy** — plus how much domain specialisation the task demands. Frontier models get the open-ended reasoning and complex generation. Our domain- and use-case-specific SLMs get the focused, repeatable work.


> *We’re not trying to choose one model size over another. We’re trying to orchestrate the right combination for each task — and, increasingly, for different stages of the same request.*


## Where NEEV comes in


Orchestration at this scale needs a common foundation, not a separate AI stack for every team. That is the role of **NEEV** , HDFC Bank’s in-house enterprise generative AI platform. NEEV provides model access, governance, orchestration and deployment capabilities in one place, so different teams can build AI applications on shared infrastructure while keeping security, regulatory compliance and operational standards consistent


For an SLM strategy, that matters. A specialised model is only useful if it can be selected, governed and deployed alongside frontier models without each team reinventing the plumbing.


## The trade-offs nobody puts on the slide


Here’s how the trade-offs have looked from where we sit.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Notice the row that isn’t there: accuracy. On a *narrow, well-defined task* , an SLM fine-tuned on our terminology, policies and workflows can perform comparably to a much larger model. Once the problem is tightly scoped, size stops being the main predictor of accuracy.


The catch is that SLMs don’t forgive sloppy engineering. A frontier model shrugs off a vague prompt; a small model may drift. So we’ve invested heavily in what we call **prompt and harness engineering** — the instructions, workflows and guardrails that sit around the model:


- **Explicit prompts.** Clearer instructions, sometimes reinforced in more than one way. We’ve found this can materially improve consistency and instruction-following.
- **Deterministic workflows.** We break one big open-ended problem into small, well-defined actions.
- **Structured outputs.** Fixed schemas, single-purpose tools, tightly scoped decision paths.
- **Validation layers.** We check the output before anything downstream trusts it.
- **Domain fine-tuning.** Real user scenarios, terminology and edge cases.


A concrete example: our customer-service triage SLM isn’t asked to “handle the customer.” It classifies the issue into a fixed set of categories, extracts specific fields, and triggers the right workflow. Small job, done fast, done the same way every time.


That’s the biggest lesson we’d pass on. The choice isn’t accuracy *versus* efficiency. It’s matching the model to the task — and then building the scaffolding that lets the smaller model punch above its weight.


## Building for how India actually talks


Our customers don’t always stay in one language during a conversation. Someone might open in Hindi, drop into English for the product name, and switch to a regional language when they need to clarify something important.

We treat that as a core design requirement, not an edge case.


Right now, most of our Indic-language work is in **voice** , where linguistic variation hits hardest. We use indigenous speech-to-text (STT) and text-to-speech (TTS) models built for multiple Indian languages and dialects, with a language model sitting in the middle as the conversational “brain.”


We design for two kinds of language preference:


- **Static** — the customer’s preferred language or dialect, known up front.
- **Dynamic** — the shifts that happen mid-conversation, which the system has to follow without making the customer “reset” their language.


For us the point isn’t translation. It’s letting people speak the way they already speak — code-switching and all — and still get an accurate, useful answer. Over time, we believe this kind of adaptation will be increasingly important for making AI accessible and effective across India’s linguistic diversity.


## What we’re seeing on cost and accuracy


In the applications we have evaluated so far, we are seeing **cost reductions of approximately 20% to 40%** compared with relying exclusively on larger frontier models.

That’s a range, not a promise — the benefits vary by use case and deployment scale.


How we keep accuracy honest matters as much as the savings. Our approach is benchmark-led:


1. **Set the bar with a frontier model.** We run the use case on a top-tier LLM first to establish a high-performance baseline.
2. **Build structured evaluations** against that baseline.
3. **Fine-tune the SLM** until it matches — or beats — the baseline on that specific task.
4. **Keep evaluating** once it’s live.


In other words, the frontier model isn’t our competition. It’s our benchmark.


The industry has started calling this way of thinking **tokenomics** : understanding the cost, performance and value created by every AI interaction. We’d push it one step further — measure *cost per intelligence* , not just cost per token. A cheap model that gets the answer wrong isn’t cheap.


## Two ways to get there


For enterprises in India, we see two complementary deployment routes:


- **India-based AI infrastructure providers** offering end-to-end inference across a range of open-source models — local infrastructure and flexible model choice, without building the whole stack.
- **Your own GPUs** , for organisations with the scale and skills. More control over data, performance, customisation and long-term unit economics, especially for steady, heavy workloads.


We expect the market to evolve toward a combination of both rather than a binary choice.


## The hidden line items


One caution: the cost comparison isn’t just inference price. Specialised SLMs can take longer to bring to market than an off-the-shelf frontier model. Budget honestly for data curation and labelling, fine-tuning, retrieval, prompt and workflow design, output validation and ongoing evaluation. For high-volume, well-defined workflows, that upfront investment can deliver stronger long-term economics, lower latency and greater control over performance.


## Sovereignty or spreadsheet? Both — in that order


It’s tempting to frame Indian SLMs as a geopolitical move. Our view is more grounded: **economics drives adoption now; sovereignty makes it durable later.**


At the enterprise level, the starting point is economics — can this AI use case pay for itself? SLMs let us take on applications that would be uneconomical at scale on frontier models alone.


But the sovereignty angle is real. Nationally, local infrastructure, models, talent and inference capacity reduce dependence on a handful of global providers. For us as an enterprise, it means tighter control over sensitive data, deployment choices, and the intellectual property built into our workflows.


NEEV, our in-house platform, reflects the same thinking. A single enterprise platform with consistent governance and security controls gives us one place to manage which models are used, how they are deployed, and how they meet regulatory requirements — rather than leaving those decisions scattered across departments.


## Is India’s compute enough?


The public numbers have moved quickly. The IndiaAI Mission was launched with an outlay of **₹10,372 crore** and has onboarded **more than 38,000 GPUs** into a common compute facility offered to startups and academia at affordable rates ([Digital India](https://www.digitalindia.gov.in/press_release/indiaai-mission-expands-ai-ecosystem-with-affordable-compute-and-startup-support/) ). Eligible users get access at up to **40% lower cost** ([CXO Digital Pulse](https://www.cxodigitalpulse.com/?p=30606) ). At the India AI Impact Summit in February 2026, the government announced **20,000 more GPUs** , taking capacity past 58,000 ([PIB](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2026/feb/doc2026217795001.pdf) ) — and later that month set a longer-term target of **200,000 GPUs** ([Angel One](https://www.angelone.in/news/economy/india-targets-200000-gpu-infrastructure-to-accelerate-ai-mission) ).


Our take: for SLMs, that capacity is a solid foundation — enough for meaningful experimentation, innovation and deployment. Building a truly indigenous *frontier-scale* model is a different matter. That would need far more high-end compute, sustained investment and long-term capacity expansion. And in modern AI, compute demand keeps growing.


## The real moat is data (and it’s messy)


If there’s one thing that separates a good SLM from a mediocre one, it’s the training data. As the country’s largest private bank, we have access to vast amounts of data, from **API call logs to voice recordings** of service conversations.


Two rules shape how we use that data:


- **Redact first.** Before anything touches a training pipeline, we strip out sensitive and personally identifiable information.
- **Label smartly.** Curating and labelling data at this scale remains a significant challenge. Our answer is a neat bit of recursion: we use *large* language models to automate the labelling that trains the *small* ones.


That’s compound AI again, this time at training time. The frontier model doesn’t just set our accuracy benchmark — it helps produce the data that lets our SLMs hit it.


## Where it’s working for us today


We’ve seen the strongest adoption in narrow, high-value workflows rather than general-purpose chat. One example is **AI voice bots** : speech-to-text on one side, text-to-speech on the other, and a specialised SLM in the middle managing the conversation, understanding intent, and securely pulling customer information through connected systems.


Here a specialised SLM can be particularly effective. We can train it on our specific customer journeys, terminology and service processes, while offering the speed, efficiency and control needed for real-time conversations.


## Can Indian SLMs compete globally?


We think the answer is a clear yes — with a qualifier about *where* .


Frontier LLMs will likely keep their edge in broad, general-purpose reasoning. But specialised, high-value applications are a different contest, and that’s where depth beats breadth.


The example closest to home for us: an indigenous SLM built around **Indian banking regulations** could outperform a much larger general-purpose model, simply because it knows local policy, compliance requirements, terminology and workflows better.


So we don’t see Indian SLMs staying niche. The opportunity is to build models that solve India’s linguistic, regulatory and enterprise problems first — and then become the best in the world at those specialised jobs.


## What we’d tell another team starting out


Looking back, what’s worked for us has been less about model size and more about engineering and business discipline:


- **Pick the model per task, not per company.** Compound AI means frontier and small models working together, sometimes in the same request.
- **Benchmark against the best, then go cheaper.** Use a frontier model to set the bar; fine-tune an SLM to clear it.
- **Engineer the harness.** Small models reward structure — explicit prompts, fixed schemas, validation, narrow tools.
- **Count every cost.** The 20–40% savings we’ve seen are real, but so are data, training and evaluation.
- **Build for how India speaks.** Code-switching isn’t an edge case; it’s the default.


The frontier race will keep making headlines. But a lot of the AI that actually reaches people in India — on a phone call, in their own mix of languages, at a cost that makes business sense — is going to be small, specialised, and very good at one thing. That’s what we’re building.
